prompt: In molecular orbital theory, what does LCAO stand for and describe?

choices.text: Linear combination of atomic orbitals: adding or subtracting atomic wavefunctions to approximate molecular ones
Localized covalent atom orbitals: orbitals that stay on one atom
choices.why: LCAO stands for linear combination of atomic orbitals, the addition or subtraction of atomic wavefunctions.

choices.text: Lewis-coupled atomic octets
choices.why: LCAO is a molecular orbital idea, not a Lewis one: molecular wavefunctions as combinations of atomic ones.

choices.text: A rule for counting valence electrons
choices.why: LCAO describes how molecular wavefunctions are built, Ψ = caψa + cbψb.

explanation: The addition or subtraction of atomic wavefunctions is termed linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO): Ψ = caψa + cbψb, where the coefficients quantify each atomic orbital's contribution to the molecular orbital.

prompt: Which is not one of the three conditions for two atomic orbitals to combine into a bond?

choices.text: The two atoms must be the same element
The atoms must be close enough for good overlap
choices.why: This is one of the three conditions: the orbitals must overlap where the probability of finding electrons is significant.

choices.text: The orbitals must have compatible symmetry
choices.why: This is one of the three conditions: same-sign regions must interfere constructively more than opposite-sign regions destructively.

choices.text: The orbitals must have similar energies
choices.why: This is one of the three conditions: orbitals close in energy give the most stable bonding orbitals.

explanation: Two atomic orbitals form a bond when (1) the atoms are close enough for good overlap (but not so close that the nuclei repel), (2) the orbitals have compatible symmetry, and (3) their energies are similar. Different elements bond all the time, as in CO and HF.

prompt: How does the energy difference between two atomic orbitals affect the bond they form?

choices.text: The larger the difference, the weaker the bonding interaction
The larger the difference, the stronger the bond
choices.why: The reverse: orbitals of similar energy combine to make the most stable bonding orbitals.

choices.text: Energy doesn't matter, only symmetry
choices.why: Symmetry and energy both matter. Orbitals with very different energies form weaker bonds.

choices.text: Orbitals must have exactly equal energies to interact at all
choices.why: Orbitals of different energies can interact, as in heteronuclear molecules, just less strongly.

explanation: Orbitals with similar energy combine to make the most stable bonding molecular orbitals. Atomic orbitals with very different energies form less stable bonding interactions, and the larger the difference, the weaker the bonding interaction.

prompt: Eight atomic orbitals combine in a molecule. How many molecular orbitals result?
explanation: The number of orbitals is conserved: combining two atomic orbitals gives two molecular orbitals, and in general the number of molecular orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals combined.

prompt: Two s orbitals combine. How do the two resulting molecular orbitals compare with the original atomic orbitals?

choices.text: The in-phase (bonding) one is lower in energy; the out-of-phase (antibonding) one is higher
Both are lower in energy
choices.why: One goes down and one goes up; the average energy stays almost constant.

choices.text: The out-of-phase one is lower in energy
choices.why: The out-of-phase combination interferes destructively, has a shorter wavelength, and is higher in energy.

choices.text: Both stay at the same energy as the atomic orbitals
choices.why: Combining splits them: a lower-energy bonding orbital and a higher-energy antibonding one.

explanation: The in-phase combination has a longer wavelength and is lower in energy (bonding); the out-of-phase combination has a shorter wavelength and is higher in energy (antibonding). Overall, the average energy and the number of wavefunctions stay about the same.

prompt: In H2, both electrons occupy the bonding orbital and the antibonding orbital is empty. What does the empty orbital contribute to the molecule's stability?

choices.text: Nothing: only occupied orbitals make a real energetic contribution
It destabilizes the molecule as much as the bonding orbital stabilizes it
choices.why: An empty antibonding orbital has no electrons, so it makes no energetic contribution. That's why H2 is stable.

choices.text: It stabilizes the molecule further
choices.why: Only occupied orbitals contribute to stability, and this one is empty.

explanation: There is an occupied and an unoccupied molecular orbital in H2; only the occupied one makes a real energetic contribution to the molecule's stability. The unoccupied orbital is "completely imaginary" until electrons are put in it.

prompt: With the N–N bond along the z axis, which pair of p orbitals overlaps end-on to form a σ bond?

choices.text: The two pz orbitals
The two px orbitals
choices.why: px orbitals are perpendicular to the bond axis, so they overlap side by side, forming π bonds.

choices.text: A px on one atom and a py on the other
choices.why: Orbitals interact with the same type on the other atom; px and py are orthogonal. End-on overlap along z uses pz.

choices.text: The two py orbitals
choices.why: py orbitals are perpendicular to the bond axis and form π bonds.

explanation: The pz orbitals lie along the bond axis, so one lobe of each overlaps strongly end-on, giving σ bonding and antibonding combinations. The px and py orbitals, orthogonal to the bond axis, form π bonds.

prompt: Which statement describes a π bond formed from two parallel p orbitals?

choices.text: It has a node along the bond axis, with electron density above and below it
Its electron density lies directly along the bond axis
choices.why: That describes a σ bond. A π bond has a node along the bond axis.

choices.text: It overlaps more strongly than a σ bond
choices.why: Side-by-side p orbitals don't overlap as strongly as orbitals lying along the bond axis.

choices.text: It is unaffected by rotating one atom relative to the other
choices.why: That's true of σ bonds. Rotating one end of a π bond breaks the overlap.

explanation: Parallel p orbitals overlap side by side, more weakly than orbitals along the bond axis. The resulting π orbitals have a node along the bond axis, with electron density above and below it.

prompt: What happens to a π bond if one atom rotates relative to the other about the bond axis?

choices.text: The p orbitals can no longer overlap, so the π connection is lost
Nothing: π bonds are symmetric about the bond axis
choices.why: π orbitals are not symmetric with respect to the bond axis. σ orbitals are.

choices.text: The π bond becomes a σ bond
choices.why: Rotation doesn't turn a π bond into a σ bond; it destroys the side-by-side overlap.

explanation: A π orbital is not symmetric with respect to the bond axis. A σ orbital is unaffected when one end rotates, but a π orbital would have to stretch to stay connected; the orbitals couldn't overlap, and the connection would be lost.

prompt: Which type of molecular orbital is typically highest in energy?

choices.text: σ*
π*
choices.why: π* orbitals are antibonding, but σ* is typically higher, because σ overlap is stronger and so splits the orbitals further.

choices.text: σ
choices.why: σ is a bonding orbital, lower in energy than the atomic orbitals.

choices.text: π
choices.why: π is a bonding orbital, below the antibonding ones.

explanation: Among σ, π, π*, and σ*, the σ* antibonding orbital is typically the highest in energy.

prompt: Why doesn't a core 1s orbital interact with a valence 2s orbital on another atom?

choices.text: Their energies are too different
They have incompatible symmetry
choices.why: Two s orbitals have compatible symmetry. The problem is the large energy difference between core and valence orbitals.

choices.text: Core orbitals don't exist in molecules
choices.why: Core orbitals still exist; they're just too low in energy to interact with valence orbitals.

explanation: For orbitals to interact, they need compatible symmetry and similar energy. The energy difference between core and valence orbitals is too large, so they cannot interact.

choices.text: Two nodes in planes containing the internuclear axis, as from two dxy orbitals
One node in a plane containing the internuclear axis
choices.why: That's a π bond. A δ bond has two such nodes.

choices.text: No node along the internuclear axis
choices.why: That's a σ bond, symmetric about the axis.

choices.text: It forms between two s orbitals
choices.why: δ bonds form between d orbitals of appropriate symmetry, such as two dxy or two dx2−y2 orbitals.

explanation: σ bonds are symmetric about the internuclear axis, π bonds have one node in a plane containing it, and δ bonds have two. With bonding along z, two dxy or two dx2−y2 orbitals can form δ bonds.

prompt: How many nodal planes containing the internuclear axis does a δ bond have?
explanation: A σ bond has none, a π bond has one, and a δ bond has two nodes in planes containing the internuclear axis.

prompt: Two atoms bond along the z axis. Which pair of d orbitals can form a σ bond?

choices.text: Two dz2 orbitals
Two dxz orbitals
choices.why: Two dxz orbitals along z form a π bond, with one node containing the axis.

choices.text: Two dxy orbitals
choices.why: Two dxy orbitals along z form a δ bond.

choices.text: A dxz on one atom and a dxy on the other
choices.why: These have incompatible symmetry along z, so they don't form bonding or antibonding orbitals.

explanation: σ bonds are symmetric about the internuclear axis. Two dz2 orbitals along z form a σ bond; d orbitals can also form σ bonds with s orbitals and certain p orbitals.

prompt: What happens when two orbitals with incompatible symmetry are brought together?

choices.text: They form no bonding or antibonding interaction
They form a weak σ bond
choices.why: Any bonding or antibonding interaction needs compatible symmetry. Incompatible orbitals give none.

choices.text: They form an antibonding orbital only
choices.why: Without compatible symmetry, there's neither bonding nor antibonding interaction.

explanation: All bonding and antibonding interactions require orbitals with compatible symmetry. Orbitals whose symmetry is incompatible with each other have no bonding or antibonding interaction.

prompt: Three atomic orbitals of compatible symmetry combine. What is the most common result?

choices.text: One bonding, one nonbonding (intermediate energy), and one antibonding orbital
Three bonding orbitals
choices.why: Orbitals aren't all lowered. With three, the usual result is one bonding, one nonbonding, and one antibonding.

choices.text: One bonding and one antibonding orbital, with one atomic orbital left unused
choices.why: The number of orbitals is conserved: three atomic orbitals give three molecular orbitals.

choices.text: Two antibonding and one bonding orbital
choices.why: The most common result is one bonding, one nonbonding of intermediate energy, and one antibonding.

explanation: When an uneven number of atomic orbitals combine, orbitals with nonbonding character form. For three, the most common result is a low-energy bonding orbital, a high-energy antibonding orbital, and a nonbonding orbital of intermediate energy.

prompt: A molecular orbital ends up very close in energy to the atomic orbital it mostly came from. What can you say about it?

choices.text: It has largely nonbonding character
It is strongly bonding
choices.why: Strongly bonding orbitals are much lower than their atomic orbitals. An MO close in energy to its atomic orbital is mostly nonbonding.

choices.text: It is strongly antibonding
choices.why: Strongly antibonding orbitals are much higher than their atomic orbitals. Closeness in energy means nonbonding character.

explanation: Bonding, nonbonding, and antibonding character exist on a spectrum. The closer a molecular orbital's energy is to its original atomic orbitals, the more nonbonding it is.

prompt: Which combination of atomic orbitals can lead to π orbitals?

choices.text: Side-by-side p + d
s + s
choices.why: Two s orbitals overlap along the axis, giving σ orbitals.

choices.text: s + p along the bond axis
choices.why: End-on s + p overlap gives σ orbitals.

choices.text: s + d
choices.why: s + d combinations give σ orbitals.

explanation: Combinations of s + s, s + p, p + p, s + d, or p + d along the bond axis can give σ orbitals. Side-by-side p + p or p + d combinations give π orbitals.
